document.wikisource_title: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy (1846)/Definitions

T1_v3: Absolute, true, and mathematical time, of itself and from its own nature, flows equably without regard to anything external, and by another name is called duration.
Relative, apparent, and common time is some sensible and external measure of duration by the means of motion, commonly used instead of true time.
All motions may be accelerated and retarded, but the true or equable progress of absolute time is liable to no change.
T2_v3: Absolute space, in its own nature, without regard to anything external, remains always similar and immovable.
Relative space is some movable dimension or measure of the absolute spaces which our senses determine by its position to bodies.
The earth may move, so that a space of our air which remains the same relative to the earth will at one time be one part of the absolute space and at another time another part.
Absolute motion is the translation of a body from one absolute place into another, and relative motion is the translation from one relative place into another.
T3_v3: Absolute, true, and mathematical time, of itself and from its own nature, flows equably without regard to anything external, and by another name is called duration.

T1_v3: Absolute, true, and mathematical time flows equably of itself without regard to anything external, and is by another name called duration.
Relative, apparent, and common time is a sensible and external measure of duration by the means of motion, such as an hour, a day, a month, a year.
It may be that there is no such thing as an equable motion whereby time may be accurately measured, though absolute time is liable to no change.
T2_v3: Absolute space in its own nature, without regard to anything external, remains always similar and immovable.
Absolute motion is the translation of a body from one absolute place into another, and relative motion is the translation from one relative place into another.
T3_v3: Absolute, true, and mathematical time flows equably of itself without regard to anything external, and is by another name called duration.
